# Hot-key results

These are deterministic load-distribution observations for three one-million-request traces. Drain time is modeled from node request counts rather than measured against a cache server.

## Environment

- Date: 2026-09-03
- Host: Apple M4, 10 logical CPUs
- OS: macOS 26.5.1, Darwin arm64
- Go: 1.26.6
- Command: `go run .`

## Experiment Variables

- Requests per workload: 1,000,000
- Logical cache keys: 10,000
- Baseline nodes: 1, 4, 16, and 64
- Replication cluster: 16 nodes
- Replicated hot keys: top 10
- Replicas per identified hot key: 4 and 16
- Assumed capacity: 100,000 requests/s per node

## Observations

Uniform traffic scaled with node count. Moving from one to 16 nodes reduced the busiest-node count from one million to 66,800, close to the mean of 62,500. At 64 nodes, finite key placement increased relative imbalance to `1.20x`, but absolute busiest-node work still fell to 18,700.

The `hot-50` trace had a 500,000-request logical key. Increasing the cluster from 16 to 64 nodes reduced the busiest-node count only from 532,502 to 509,300. The extra nodes redistributed cold-key traffic but could not split the 500,000 requests for the single-copy hot key.

Zipf traffic showed the same bound less dramatically. Its hottest key received 207,632 requests. At 64 nodes, the busiest node still received 213,438 requests while the mean was only 15,625, producing a `13.66x` max-to-mean ratio.

Replicating the ten identified hot keys changed the routing unit. With 16 replicas on 16 nodes, the busiest-node count fell to 89,465 for Zipf and 64,661 for `hot-50`. The busiest physical copy of the 500,000-request key received 31,823 requests, close to an even one-sixteenth split.

## Caveats

- Minimum drain time is request count divided by an assumed 100,000 requests/s; no cache server or network was benchmarked.
- All requests are reads and all requested values are available. Replica invalidation, writes, misses, and expiry are absent.
- The ten hottest keys are known before routing begins. Detection lag can leave a production hotspot unmitigated during its most important interval.
- Hash and replica routing are deterministic. Other placement functions change exact node counts but not the indivisible-key constraint.
- Zipf observations depend on the exponent, finite key count, request count, and seed.
